sections.h2: Where does a Washington County, PA deed get recorded?
sections.html:
At the Recorder of Deeds office in the Crossroads Center, 95 W. Beau St., Suite 520, Washington, PA 15301; the number is 724-228-6806. Staff are in from 9:00 a.m. until 4:30 p.m., though the 4:00 p.m. mark is the real deadline, because recording itself stops then.

The office dates from 1781, the year the county was cut out of Westmoreland County. By its own account it records deeds, mortgages, subdivision plans and other papers the state treats as permanent, collects the fees and taxes attached to them, and sends the receipts on to the state, the county, the municipalities and the school districts. Everything is indexed, verified and scanned the same business day.

A Washington County sale ends at this counter. The deed is signed at closing and then recorded here, which is the moment the buyer's name enters the public record. To see what is already on file against a property, search Landex, which holds every deed from 1781 to the present, or sit at one of the public computers in the office.

sections.h2: What does the Washington County recorder charge to record a deed?
sections.html:
The base fee depends on document type, and every base fee already covers four pages, four indexed names and one PIN. The county posts a fee schedule and a fee calculator on the recorder page, so check the current figure there before you write a check.

Washington County recorder charges on top of the base fee, from the county recorder page
ItemCharge
Included in the base fee4 pages, 4 indexed names, 1 PIN
Each additional page$2.00
Each additional indexed name$0.50
Each additional PIN$10.00
CJEA surcharge after the fiscal code changeUp from $2.50 to $3.50, a $1 increase

The county explains that the printed schedule lags behind the $1 CJEA increase, so a recent schedule on the site may show a figure $1 lower than what the counter collects. If the total is unclear, the office asks you to call 724-228-6806 rather than guess.

Two small details catch people out. The PIN charge applies per parcel number, so a sale that combines several parcels costs more than a single-lot sale. And the extra-page charge adds up on long documents, such as a deed that carries a full legal description and several exhibits.

sections.h2: Who pays realty transfer tax on a Washington County sale?
sections.html:
Both do, in the eyes of the state. The Pennsylvania Department of Revenue sets the commonwealth tax at 1 percent of the value transferred and makes grantor and grantee jointly and severally liable, so the state can pursue either party for the whole amount.

County recorders collect that share and usually a local share too, then pass the money along. Washington County's page lists the state, county, municipalities and school districts as the recipients, which means the local rate follows the municipality. Get the combined rate from the recorder or your closing agent before you settle on a net price.

  • Exempt transfers include some between relatives, some to government bodies, and property passing under a will or by intestacy.
  • An exemption claim normally needs paperwork, so ask the office which form goes with the deed.
  • Who bears the cost is a term of the sale contract, not something the recorder decides.

sections.h2: What formatting rules can get a Washington County document rejected?
sections.html:
Page size and type size are the two that the county stresses on its recorder page. The office no longer accepts legal-size pages electronically, and it sets minimum fonts: 12 point on letter-size pages and 14 point on legal-size pages.

Subdivision plans follow their own rules. They are filed on paper or mylar, and they need signatures from the Washington County Planning Commission, the local planning commission where one applies, the board of supervisors or borough council, and the owners of the land being divided. The plan also carries an engineer's seal, and it has to be recorded within 90 days of the local governing body's approval.

  • Check page size before you scan a deed for e-recording.
  • Confirm the type size on a long exhibit, since small print is a common reason for a bounce.
  • For a plan, count the 90 days from the local approval, not from the date you finish the drawings.

sections.h2: What is Washington County like for a house sale?
sections.html:
It is a large, mostly owner-occupied county south of Pittsburgh. QuickFacts credits it with 210,802 residents in 2025 on 857 square miles of land, plus 99,340 housing units and 88,505 households in the 2020 to 2024 survey.

About 76.1 percent of households own where they live. Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $228,500, rent runs a median $949, and the typical household earns $78,958. People with a mortgage pay a median $1,618 a month in housing costs.

Washington is the county seat and Monongahela the only other city. Canonsburg and Charleroi are two of the larger boroughs, and Peters Township is the biggest municipality. Washington & Jefferson College is in the city of Washington, coal mining continues at the Enlow Fork mine, and the Southpointe business park spreads over more than 800 acres. About 37.8 inches of snow fall in a typical year, mostly from November to April, so buyers touring an older house will look hard at the roof and the furnace.

sections.h2: Which school districts and towns shape buyer demand in Washington County?
sections.html:
Canon-McMillan, Peters Township, Charleroi, Burgettstown Area and Chartiers-Houston are among the districts that draw different groups of buyers. The county is split into many small districts, so neighbors on opposite sides of a boundary can pay different school taxes.

For that reason, a listing in Washington County sells better when it names the district. Peters Township is the largest municipality, and Charleroi is a river borough named after the Belgian city, because Belgian glassmakers settled the Monongahela area in the late 1800s. The countywide median home value of $228,500 hides a lot of variation, so look at recent sales inside the specific district.

sections.h2: What if the house has unpaid taxes before the deed is recorded?
sections.html:
Two county offices share the work. The Treasurer collects county taxes at 95 W. Beau St., Suite 130, 724-228-6780, with the counter open 9:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. The Tax Revenue Department, in Suite 525 at 724-228-6850, handles both assessments and delinquent claims.

Since October 6, 2025 the Treasurer has refused personal checks for delinquent taxes. Certified checks, money orders, cash and cards are accepted. Paying online adds a charge: 2.50 percent with a $2.00 minimum on cards, or $1.50 for an electronic check.

When back taxes are attached to the house you plan to sell, request a written balance from Tax Revenue ahead of closing so your closing agent can settle it from the proceeds. Washington County also has a Board of Assessment Appeals, and Tax Revenue can describe the filing steps.

faqs.q: What time does the Washington County recorder stop accepting deeds?
faqs.a: Recording ends at 4:00 p.m., half an hour before the office closes. The address is 95 W. Beau St., Suite 520, Washington. A deed that shows up after 4:00 p.m. is held for the next business day.

faqs.q: Can I record a legal-size deed electronically in Washington County?
faqs.a: No. The county says it no longer accepts legal-size pages electronically. Letter-size pages need at least 12 point type and legal-size pages need at least 14 point, so bring a paper original if the document is on legal paper.

faqs.q: Does a Washington County deed fee cover extra pages and names?
faqs.a: The base fee covers four pages, four indexed names and one PIN. Each page beyond four costs $2.00, each extra name $0.50 and each extra PIN $10.00, and the county added $1 to its CJEA surcharge, so confirm the total by phone at 724-228-6806.

faqs.q: How can I look up recorded deeds in Washington County, PA?
faqs.a: Use Landex online, which holds deeds from 1781 to the present, or use the public computers inside the Recorder of Deeds office. Landex support is 1-800-370-2836, option 4, according to the county page.

faqs.q: Who owes the transfer tax when a Washington County house sells?
faqs.a: Both sides are liable. Pennsylvania charges 1 percent of the value transferred and holds buyer and seller jointly responsible, and a local tax normally rides along. The sale contract decides who pays in practice; the recorder can confirm the local rate.
